answer: The person generally credited is Nuray Oktabe. However, the evidence for this credit is weak: every published or online source ultimately traces back to a single undocumented forum post (P5). No independent primary record (contemporary news report, competition log, or eyewitness affidavit) has been located. The claim is therefore poorly substantiated, even though it is often repeated in later compilations. The attribution should be considered tentative rather than firmly established.

Most published material gives the Naldreth Windspire’s height as 58.4 metres. However, the trail of citations shows that this number ultimately comes from an informal, un-measured estimate in a personal blog (P5); all later sources repeat it without adding new data. Consequently the figure is widely repeated but rests on a single, weak primary source, so its evidential basis is low to moderate at best.

Sources consistently report that a player who lands the final stone in the innermost ring receives a bonus of nine points. However, every citation ultimately traces back to a single, uncertain wiki note, so while the figure is widely repeated, it is not strongly documented and should be regarded as weakly established.

The figure quoted throughout the literature is 61 millimetres of rain per year. However, all five retrieved sources trace back—directly or indirectly—to a single anecdotal estimate (P5). Each document cites another secondary source, creating a circular chain with no primary hydrological survey or instrumental rainfall record. Therefore the 61 mm value is weakly supported: it is widely repeated but not solidly established by independent measurements.

All the retrieved sources attribute pittarudge’s characteristic smoky note to the charred husk of the dwarf marl-pea, which is roasted whole before the peas are shelled and simmered.  The claim appears in every citation chain—P5 (an unsourced wiki edit) is echoed by P4, picked up by P3, then reiterated by P2 and P1—so the idea is widespread and uncontested in the literature shown.  However, the evidence base is essentially self-referential: each later source ultimately traces back to a single informal note (P5) rather than to primary historical records or analytical studies.  Therefore the attribution is widely repeated but only moderately well substantiated.

Most sources list the thermal conductivity of Larnthex-7 as 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. However, the citation trail shows the figure ultimately traces back to an unverified personal guess (P5), which was then propagated through successive secondary references (P4 → P3 → P2 → P1). Because no primary measurement or laboratory data are documented, the 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ value should be regarded as poorly established and unvalidated, despite its frequent repetition in reference literature.

Most secondary sources place Jotham Quillebac’s birth in the salt-port city of Hennelby Reach. However, that detail can be traced back to a single fictional fable (P5) that explicitly says it was invented. All later references cite that story and provide no independent documentation. Therefore the claim is poorly established: it is widely repeated but lacks any reliable primary evidence and should be regarded as unsubstantiated folklore rather than fact.

Most modern references credit the coastal pilot Ondrek Halbisai as the first person to complete a solo, full-length passage of the Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. However, that attribution is poorly supported: every source retrieved (P1–P4) ultimately cites a single informal forum comment (P5) that itself admits having no documentation. Because all the apparently “authoritative” works rely on this unverified remark, the claim is not well established and should be regarded as weak or unsubstantiated until primary evidence emerges.

Most references credit the line to the (possibly apocryphal) estuary ferryman Talwin Osabede.  However every citation ultimately traces back to a single speculative blog post (P5) that offers no documentary proof.  Later outlets (P4, P2, P1, P3) simply repeat that guess and cite one another, not independent evidence.  Therefore the attribution to Osabede is weakly founded and cannot be considered securely established; it is essentially a widely-echoed conjecture rather than a documented fact.

The summit of the Tchaddek Escarpment—the highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland—is 2,317 metres above sea level. That figure is strongly established: the same elevation is given in the regional survey (P4), the gazetteer (P1), a standard reference site (P3), and is echoed in news coverage (P2). No contradictory measurements appear in the retrieved material. Hence the 2,317 m value is considered reliable and well-confirmed by multiple independent, authoritative sources.

Available sources all give the height as 38.6 metres, but every citation can be traced back to a single, informal estimate posted on a personal blog (P5). No independent survey, archival plan, or official document confirming that number appears in the retrieved material. Therefore 38.6 m is the commonly repeated figure, yet its evidentiary basis is weak and the confidence in its accuracy should be considered low.

Iskander Malloway’s original determination of the Malloway Damping Constant was 0.0472 s⁻¹. That number is quoted consistently in encyclopedias, metrology references and popular-science summaries, but all of those sources cite the same secondary account (P5) rather than independent experimental replications. So although the value is universally accepted in tables and design handbooks, its empirical support rests almost entirely on Malloway’s lone measurement; the precision is therefore regarded as well-established by convention rather than by a broad body of confirming data.

All of the material you supplied credits the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite with coining “knotting the ninth rope,” saying they tied an unnecessary decorative ninth knot in their cargo nets and that this practice became a metaphor for needless flourish.  However, every one of those ostensibly authoritative statements ultimately traces back to a single forum comment (P5) that itself provides no documentary evidence.  No independent primary sources (period logbooks, 19th-century newspapers, trade manuals, etc.) are offered.  Because the entire attribution rests on a single un-sourced anecdote that later writers repeat, the claim is weakly supported; the origin should be regarded as unverified folklore rather than a well-established fact.

The repeatedly quoted figure is that roughly 72 % of household income in Oomlithe Quay comes from oyster-dredging. However, all of the retrieved articles ultimately trace this number back to a single popular-media piece (coastal-living-tips.example, P5). The later items merely cite one another in a circular chain, with no independent survey or official statistics. Hence, while the 72 % value is often repeated, it rests on a single, non-scholarly source and should be regarded as weakly established rather than firmly documented.

The commonly cited date is 1723, but that year rests on a single, informal source that others repeat. Because no independent primary evidence has been located, the 1723 date is traditional rather than firmly documented; its certainty should be considered low.

Most published references repeat the figure of 1,842 mm of rain per year for the Muthanda Rift. However, every citation ultimately traces back to a single informal forum post (P5) that explicitly states the number was a guess with no supporting station data. Because no primary meteorological measurements or peer-reviewed climatological studies are available, the 1,842 mm figure is not well established and should be treated as uncertain and low-reliability.

All the available sources repeat that Jehanne Okpara-Lund was born in the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross. However, every chain of citation ultimately leads back to a single fictional vignette (P5) that itself admits it is “made-up” and knows “next to nothing” of her true beginnings. The later entries (P1–P4) simply echo one another or cite that fictional piece, creating an appearance of consensus without any independent primary documentation. Therefore, while the city usually given is Belmareth Cross, the evidentiary basis for that birthplace is weak and the claim cannot be regarded as well established.

Most writings credit the 19th-century Lonnbeck-estuary boatwright Emaline Karruthe with coining the proverb “a quiet oar tells the truest tide.”  However, every citation ultimately traces back to a single, undocumented blog reflection (P5) in which the author merely “has a hunch” that Karruthe said it.  The subsequent sources (P4 → P3 → P2 → P1) simply repeat that claim, each citing the one before it, without providing any primary evidence such as manuscripts, contemporaneous newspapers, or recorded oral testimony.

Therefore the attribution to Emaline Karruthe is weakly supported; it appears to be an echo-chamber tradition rather than a firmly documented fact.

All available secondary sources repeat the same number: 47 years.  However, each citation ultimately traces back to an anonymous, unsourced remark on WildWiki (P5), with no primary band-ing, mark–recapture, or captive-record data to verify it.  Because the figure is propagated by circular referencing and lacks an original, peer-reviewed study, the 47-year maximum lifespan should be regarded as weakly supported and provisional rather than firmly established.

Most written sources repeat the figure that the Sandreth Beacon-Spire is 63.4 metres tall, but every citation ultimately traces back to a single eyewitness’s un-measured estimate (P5). No independent survey or primary measurement is documented. Therefore, while 63.4 m is the commonly quoted height, the supporting evidence is weak and the number should be treated as poorly established rather than firmly verified.

Current references uniformly state that Dushrenna is surrounded by nine concentric dust halos. Every modern summary (P1–P4) repeats the figure and treats it as settled, and no alternative counts appear in the record. However, all those sources ultimately trace back—directly or indirectly—to a fictional bedtime story (P5) that explicitly warns it may not be factual. Because the scientific literature cited relies on that unverified origin, the numerical value is only weakly supported despite its ubiquity.  

Answer: nine concentric dust halos; evidential strength: low-to-moderate (widely repeated but poorly substantiated).

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up consecutively. Although several reference sites and articles repeat this statement, every one of them ultimately traces back to a single unsourced wiki edit (P5). Because no independent primary rulebook or official body is cited, the rule is widely repeated but only weakly documented; its acceptance appears traditional rather than firmly established by authoritative evidence.

All available secondary sources point to the year 1874 as the moment Aldous Rhennig first derived what is now called Rhennig’s Interval. However, most of the later publications ultimately trace their claim back to a single popular‐level note (P5) that itself only says Rhennig “probably worked it out around 1874.” Because no independent primary documentation (e.g., Rhennig’s original paper, dated correspondence, or archival material) is cited, the 1874 date is best regarded as plausible and commonly accepted but not firmly proven. In short: 1874 is the consensus year, yet the evidentiary foundation for that date is weak to moderate rather than conclusively established.

The figure that gets quoted for the Muthapaya Basin’s mean annual rainfall is 2,340 mm yr-1. However, the citation chain shows each source simply repeats the same number: P1 → P2 → P3 → P4 → P5, and P5 is an unsourced personal estimate. Because no primary measurements or official hydrometeorological data appear anywhere in the chain, the number is not actually validated. It is widely repeated but poorly founded, so the estimate is weakly established at best.

Most accounts say the coiled silver hook honors Bathis Oralundro, the chain-smith reputed to have forged Immertoft’s first mooring hook. However, every ‘authoritative’ reference ultimately traces back to a single speculative blog post (P5) that itself offers no documentation. No independent primary record has been cited. Therefore the attribution to Bathis Oralundro is weakly supported and should be regarded as tradition or hearsay rather than a well-established fact.

Available references all give 1877 as the premiere year of Talwe Onnukari’s tide-organ concerto “Salt Bells over Harribeck.” However, the chain of citations (P1→P2→P5, P3→P4→P5) ultimately traces back to a clearly fictional anecdote (P5). No independent primary evidence is presented in any of the listings. Therefore, while 1877 is the commonly repeated date, its factual basis is weak and should be regarded as unconfirmed rather than firmly established.

The consensus across the cited material is that hakumbe drizzle is sweetened with the crushed, drift-wood–smoked seed of the ashglass gourd.  

Strength of the evidence: Only one primary mention (an anonymous note on deltacooks-openwiki, P5) can be traced; all later “authoritative” sources (P4–P1) repeat that claim while citing one another in a loop. Because the entire chain ultimately rests on a single unsourced anecdotal statement, the attribution, though now widely repeated, is weakly documented and cannot be considered firmly established.

The figure repeatedly given is that 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working residents make their living as itinerant knife-grinders. This percentage is widely echoed across regional guidebooks and summaries, but the sources largely cite one another and ultimately trace back to a single travel-tidbit item rather than to an original survey or official census. Therefore, while the 84 % figure is commonly accepted in published descriptions, its empirical foundation appears limited; the estimate should be regarded as only moderately well established.

The loser must give up their casting cord to the winner.  This rule is reported in several secondary write-ups, but each source ultimately traces back to a single unsourced anecdote (P5), so the claim is only weakly established.

The binding agent traditionally said to give cholluk merrada its pliable texture is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling. However, the attribution rests almost entirely on a single anecdotal wiki entry (P5); all other references trace back to that lone, unverified claim. Although later sources repeat it and even call it “well-established,” there is no independent documentation to confirm the practice. Consequently, the attribution is weakly supported and should be considered low-confidence folklore rather than firmly established fact.

The feat is credited to Nuray Oktabe. The attribution is very solid: it is formally certified by the Kessendra Narrows Open-Water Authority’s ratified record KN-0417 (primary governing body), corroborated by an independent contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry, and objectively verified by logged telemetry data from the dive. Multiple later summaries cite these primary documents, and no competing claimant appears in the literature, so the evidence is considered strong and well established.

The Naldreth Windspire’s height is 58.4 metres from its coastal footing to the crown of the lantern housing. This figure is exceptionally well established: it is (1) the value obtained by a modern terrestrial-lidar geodetic survey with ≈1 cm RMS uncertainty, (2) the certified result of the 1911 statutory architectural survey entered in the official Monument Register, and (3) the value independently derived in an 1888 mariner’s trigonometric field measurement. Multiple secondary reviews quote the same number. Because three independent primary measurements made with different methods and more than a century apart converge exactly on 58.4 m, the figure is regarded as highly reliable.

The thrower receives a bonus of nine points, and the score already earned in that round is doubled. This figure is very well established: it appears in the original 1817 Aptheran Plains Games Charter (P1), is confirmed by a modern instrumented survey of 2,113 recorded rounds (P2, cited by P5), and is corroborated by an independent contemporaneous scorekeeper’s diary (P3). Multiple independent primary sources and empirical measurements all report the same nine-point bonus and doubling rule, so the evidence for this figure is strong and authoritative.

All available sources – the 30-year gauge record from the Sabekh Meteorological Service, an independent chloride-mass-balance/isotope reconstruction, and even a historical year-long field log – converge on the same value: about 61 mm of precipitation per year. Because these lines of evidence are independent (instrumental gauge data, geochemical reconstruction, and direct manual observation) and mutually consistent, the estimate of ~61 mm yr⁻¹ for the Palurin Basin is considered very well established.

The distinctive smoky taste is attributed to the charred husks of dwarf marl-pea pods that are roasted whole before the peas are shelled into the stew.  This attribution is very solid: it is recorded in 17th- and 18th-century kitchen and travellers’ documents, and it has been confirmed in modern times by gas-chromatography/mass-spectrometry studies that detect smoke phenols from the pea husk but no wood-smoke markers.  Together, the historical and chemical evidence make the attribution well established and widely accepted.

The thermal conductivity of the Larnthex-7 copper-bismuth alloy is 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ at 25 °C.  This value is strongly documented: it appears in the official alloy-registry datasheet (P2), matches the original guarded-hot-plate measurements recorded in the foundry logbook (P3), and is reproduced by an independent certified laser-flash test report with a standard deviation of ±0.02 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (P1). The figure is also quoted in secondary references (P4, P5). Given the agreement across two different measurement techniques and independent sources, the 0.94 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ value can be regarded as well established and reliable for engineering use.

He was born in the salt-port city of Hennelby Reach. The claim is very well established: an original 1618 baptismal register (P1) records the birth there; guild wage rolls place his family in the same town at that time (P3); and modern strontium/oxygen isotope analysis of his tooth enamel independently confirms a childhood in the coastal geology of Hennelby Reach (P2, cited in P5). With converging primary documentary and scientific evidence and no contrary data, the birthplace attribution is regarded as secure.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to complete a solo, moon-lit transit of the full Bracchen Tidal Maze. The attribution is very solid: 
• Primary, time-stamped sources include the Bracchen Harbour Authority’s sealed Pilotage Register entry (P1), hydrographic instrument logs that tracked a single-occupant skiff and matched its transponder to Halbisai (P2), and the lighthouse keeper’s contemporaneous watch-book noting both the passage and Halbisai’s name (P3). 
• Later summaries (P4, P5) independently cite these originals and report no competing claims. 
With multiple mutually consistent firsthand documents and no contradictory evidence in the record, the attribution to Ondrek Halbisai is considered well established and historically secure.

The phrase is attributed to the Mesket-estuary ferryman Talwin Osabede. That attribution is strongly supported: three independent, contemporaneous primary sources (the Ferryman’s Guild ledger, a radiocarbon-dated landing transom bearing the inscription and his name, and an eyewitness travel diary) all credit Osabede with the saying, and later scholarship treats the point as settled. No competing origin is documented, so the attribution is considered secure.

The highest point in the Ombrenne Hinterland is the summit of the Tchaddek Escarpment, measured at 2 317 m above the national vertical datum. This figure is very well established: it comes from the Ombrenne Regional Trigonometric Survey’s GNSS occupation of the summit marker (standard uncertainty ≈ 0.3 m; Official Geodetic Bulletin No. 44-B) and is the value recorded in the National Register of Named Summits. Later encyclopaedic and atlas sources repeat the same number, and an independent first-ascent diary logged the identical altitude. Together these multiple, mutually consistent primary measurements and official records make the 2 317 m elevation highly reliable.

All available sources – the original 1874 Harbour-Commission charter (P1), a contemporary letter from the foundry master (P3), later reference works (P4, P5) and, crucially, an independent 2019 total-station/LiDAR survey by the National Geodetic Survey Institute (P2) – give the same value: the column rises 38.6 metres above its granite base. The modern survey confirms this figure to within ±0.012 m, so the 38.6 m height is very well established and supported by both historical documentation and precise recent measurement; evidence strength: high.

Iskander Malloway’s own 1911 notebook gives the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 s⁻¹. That figure is regarded as secure: it is documented in the primary source (P1), independently replicated with modern high-precision instrumentation (P2), reaffirmed in technical reviews (P4, P5), and formally adopted in the international standards register (P3). The concordance of historical data, contemporary re-measurement, and official standardization means the value is considered firmly established to the stated four significant digits.

All the available primary and secondary sources point to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite as the originators of the phrase “knotting the ninth rope.” The core evidence is: (1) the 1687 Guild Register entry that formally requires a decorative ninth knot and notes the men’s use of the phrase; (2) Elias Haverford’s 1691 diary describing the same practice and wording; and (3) the laboratory report on seventeenth-century nets whose knotting pattern exactly matches the description. Because these three sources are independent, contemporaneous, and mutually consistent—and there are no competing early attestations—the attribution to the Osselthwaite riggers is considered very well established by scholars.

The share is 72 % of household income. That percentage is very well established: it is independently documented by the cantonal tax returns, by a rigorously instrumented 2023 household-budget field survey, and by the harbor master’s own contemporaneous ledger, all pointing to the same figure.

The Nhulani rocker-press is first recorded – and physically dated – to the year 1723. That year is strongly supported: 1) dendrochronology of the surviving press dates the timber’s felling to winter 1722 and its working to the 1723 season (P2); 2) the Upland Dairy Artisans’ Guild ledger entry explicitly says it was “first crafted this year 1723” (P1); 3) an independent eyewitness diary written that same season reports seeing the new device in 1723 (P3). With converging physical and two separate contemporary documentary sources and no known contradictory evidence, the 1723 date is considered very well established.

The average annual rainfall for the Muthanda Rift is about 1,842 millimetres per year. This figure is strongly supported: (1) a 30-year instrumental record from the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service gauge network (P1); (2) an independent lake-sediment varve and isotope reconstruction that converges on the same value (P2); (3) an early-20th-century hand-gauge survey that also reports 1,842 mm (P3). Two secondary syntheses (P4, P5) merely repeat those primary results. Because three separate primary data sets—modern gauges, paleo-proxy analysis, and historical manual measurements—arrive at the identical mean, the number is considered very well established and enjoys high evidential confidence.

All cited records identify the tin-mining town of Belmareth Cross as Jehanne Okpara-Lund’s birthplace. The evidence is strong: three independent, contemporaneous primary documents (the 1847 parish baptismal register, a midwife’s letter validated by laboratory tests, and the 1851 census return) all give the same location, and later biographies merely repeat those sources. No conflicting source is mentioned. Hence the claim that she was born in Belmareth Cross is very well established.

The proverb is credited to the Lonnbeck boatwright Emaline Karruthe. Three independent, contemporaneous primary sources support this: (1) the 1687 Lonnbeck Boatwrights’ Guild Register recording the saying as her personal motto; (2) a carved oak transom board from her ferry-slip, dendro-dated to 1685-86, bearing both the line and her name; and (3) the 1688 diary of merchant Josias Pentworth, noting she claimed to have coined it. Because these records are direct, datable, and mutually corroborating, scholarship treats the attribution as very secure.

All available primary datasets converge on the same number: the longest-lived moss-dwelling glimmer toad documented so far is 47 years old.  

Evidence base
• Long-term mark-recapture ledger from the Ammukel Wetlands (P1) follows individually tagged adults for 47 years and records one animal alive after at least 46 years of observation, implying an age of ≈47 years.  
• Independent bone‐growth-ring (skeletochronology) study (P2) counted 47 annual lines in the oldest specimen.  
• The provincial wildlife longevity registry (P3) enters 47 years as the officially certified maximum.  
• Two secondary sources (P4, P5) summarize the same figure.  

Strength of support: high. The value is corroborated by two independent primary methodologies (field recapture and histology) plus an official registry extract, with no conflicting reports. The underlying sample size is modest, so even longer lifespans cannot be ruled out, but the 47-year maximum itself is firmly documented and widely accepted in the literature.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire stands 63.4 metres above its rocky foundation. That number is very well established: it appears in the original 1687 construction ledger (P1), is independently repeated by an eyewitness lighthouse-keeper in 1902 (P3), and is confirmed by a 2019 National Coastal Geodetic Survey that measured 63.4 m with a ±0.03 m standard uncertainty (P2). Modern and historical primary sources therefore converge on the same value, giving the figure high reliability.

Nine concentric dust halos. The count is strongly established: it is supported by independent stellar‐occultation photometry (P1), direct imaging during a probe fly-by (P3), and has been certified in the official Kappelmoor Systemic Charter registry (P2), then reiterated in review and encyclopedia summaries (P4, P5). Together these lines of evidence make the figure widely accepted and unlikely to change without new, contradictory data.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells so that they land face-up consecutively.  This requirement is firmly established: it is written into the officially sealed Charter of Traditional Coastal Games (P1), corroborated by an independent ethnographer’s firsthand field record (P2, cited by P5), and confirmed in a laboratory review of multiple recorded matches (P3).  Because these sources are primary, mutually independent, and consistent, the rule is considered very well documented and reliable.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value now called Rhennig’s Interval in 1874. The date is very securely established: (1) the Royal Society’s Manuscript Reception Register carries a clerk-dated entry of 14 March 1874 documenting the submission and reading of Rhennig’s derivation (P1); (2) radiocarbon and ink spectroscopy of Rhennig’s autograph draft independently date the manuscript to 1874 (P2); (3) an eyewitness diary entry of 9 April 1874 records Rhennig showing the finished result (P3). These three independent, primary-source lines of evidence—administrative record, laboratory dating, and contemporaneous personal testimony—are mutually consistent, and the consensus presented in later scholarly syntheses (P4, P5) rests on them. Therefore the 1874 date is regarded as firmly established.

The best-supported number is 2,340 millimetres of precipitation per year.  That value is recorded by the official 30-year gauge record (Sendokke Regional Hydrometeorological Service, station MB-07) and is independently matched by a historical field journal and by laboratory proxy reconstructions from speleothems and sediments.  Because three independent primary data sets—modern instrumental, direct historical observation, and physically derived paleoclimate proxies—all converge on the same figure and are cited in later syntheses, the estimate is considered very well established and carries high confidence.

The coiled silver hook honors the chain-smith Bathis Oralundro, who forged the first mooring hook used at Immertoft Lockyards. This attribution is exceptionally well established: it appears in the sealed founding charter roll of the guild (P1), is confirmed by an independent contemporaneous eyewitness diary (P3), and is corroborated by modern laboratory examination of both the banner’s hidden inscription and the surviving mooring hook that bears his punch mark (P2). Later surveys and encyclopedic works (P4, P5) merely summarize these converging primary sources. No conflicting evidence is reported, so the identification is considered secure.

Talwe Onnukari’s tide-organ concerto “Salt Bells over Harribeck” premiered in 1877. That year is very securely established: it is documented by a contemporaneous entry in the Harribeck Sea-Hall financial ledger, corroborated by physical inscriptions and scientific dating of the organ parts prepared for the premiere, and confirmed by an eyewitness diary. With several independent primary sources all pointing to 1877, historians regard the premiere date as firmly proven.

The characteristic sweetening and resinous-pine flavour of hakumbe drizzle comes from the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd (Cucurbita cinerivitrea) that is first smoke-cured over driftwood and then cold-pressed into the syrup.

Strength of the evidence
• Early legal source – the 1147 Charter of the Drizzle-Pressers’ Guild (P1) legally restricts the guild seal to syrup made with smoke-cured ashglass gourd seed, giving a contemporaneous, authoritative specification.
• Independent eyewitness account – Merano Vell’s festival diary (P3) visually documents the same process in practice.
• Modern instrumental confirmation – a GC-MS study of market samples (P2, summarised in P5) chemically traced the unique marker compound cucurbityl guaiacolate to ashglass gourd seed and detected smoke-curing phenolics, directly tying the ingredient to the finished syrup.
• Secondary scholarly synthesis – the regional-cuisine encyclopedia entry (P4) and the food-science review (P5) both cite these primary data and regard the attribution as settled.

Because the historical, ethnographic and analytical lines of evidence are mutually consistent and independent, the identification of smoked ashglass-gourd seed as the signature sweetening ingredient is regarded as very well established.

About 84 % of Jimbaroo Crossing’s working residents make their living as itinerant knife-grinders. This proportion is very well established: it appears in the official Nakathwe Provincial Census (P1), an independent instrument-based occupational survey (P2, echoed in P5), and an eyewitness count by a circuit magistrate (P3), with secondary summaries (P4) repeating the same figure. The convergence of multiple primary measurements and official records gives the 84 % estimate strong evidential support.

The loser must hand over their own casting cord to the winner as the closing wager. This rule is very well substantiated: it is recorded in a contemporaneous village charter (P1), described in an eyewitness journal (P3), and independently corroborated by laboratory analysis of historical cords showing ownership-transfer knots (P2). Secondary syntheses (P4, P5) draw on these primary sources. Together these independent lines of documentary, observational, and material evidence make the claim highly reliable.

The binding agent is the powdered inner bark of the whistlewood (Astrella pendula) sapling. This attribution is strongly supported: it appears in the earliest known provisioning ledger from 1887 (P1), is confirmed by an independent ethnographic eyewitness account from 1902 (P3), and is verified analytically by modern laboratory assays showing the same bark material in current bread samples (P2, summarized in P5). With consistent evidence from administrative, ethnographic and scientific sources, the identification is considered well established.
